newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ex-banker takes Sinn Fein into Irish parliament.
newsitem.headline: Ex-banker takes Sinn Fein into Irish parliament.

text.p: A dapper one-time banker on Thursday took his seat in the Irish parliament for Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA guerrillas, for the first time in modern Irish history.
Caoimhghin O'Caolain told the house that he looked forward to the day when Britain's six-county Northern Ireland would be reunited with the Irish republic.

Watched by Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, O'Caolain said he looked forward to the day when the three would sit "in a national parliament for a 32-county Ireland".

Adams and McGuinness were both elected to the British parliament on May 1 but declined to take their seats because it would have entailed an oath of allegiance to Britain and its rule of Northern Ireland.
Sinn Fein followed a similar policy towards the Irish parliament until the mid-1980s when it reversed its policy.
O'Caolain said he would be backing the minority government of Bertie Ahern, the Fianna Fail leader who was set to become Prime Minister after a parliamentary vote later on Thursday.
Ahern has promised to make Northern Ireland a priority and to work with Britain's new Prime Minister, Tony Blair, to get all sides to the negotiating table including Sinn Fein.
O'Caolain made no reference to the ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army which Ahern and Blair and U.S. President Bill Clinton demand as the price of Sinn Fein's entry to the peace talks.
All three governments sent Sinn Fein into the wilderness in 1996 after its IRA allies ended a 17-month ceasefire and bombed London in a renewed war to end British rule of Northern Ireland.

Sinn Fein shares the IRA's goals of merging Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic, but it remains barred from multi-party talks on the province's future because the IRA has not restored its ceasefire.

It says it is determined to end the 28-year conflict, which has claimed 3,200 lives, and says O'Caolain was involved in the drive for peace. One of his main roles was lobbying U.S. opinion to win support for Sinn Fein's cause.

O'Caolain said his election victory demonstrated a "clear acceptance and understanding of the central role Sinn Fein has played in an earnest endeavour to ensure that we have an inclusive peace process in place."

But in the deprived estates of Monaghan which provided the core of his support, O'Caolain was elected as much for his promises to fight unemployment, win investment for the region and solve the day-to-day problems of local people as for his republican ideals.

"The issue of Northern Ireland hardly arises at all," wrote an Irish Times reporter who accompanied him on the campaign trail. "In some doorways, women dressed in the council house uniform of baggy tee-shirts and leggings bring up problems with rent allowances or defective windows."
Married with four children, O'Caolain left banking in the 1980s to become a county councillor and community activist.
His fondness for sharp suits has become his trademark. "O'Caolain still looks the part of the senior bank official he used to be," the Irish Times said.
